content: Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about the Get Real website to understand what it should do and how it should support high-school students. Before we begin, are you comfortable with this interview scope, or would you expect us to cover something different?

Yes, that scope sounds right. We’re focused on the website as a way to help high-school students explore computer science, understand what the degree and careers look like, and feel more confident about taking the next step. If we uncover related details along the way, that’s fine, but that’s the core of what we need.
To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m here on behalf of the Oregon University System team working on the Get Real website. My connection is mainly around making sure the site meets the needs of the students we’re trying to reach and supports the broader goal of getting more high-school students interested in computer science.
Thanks. Could you describe the current Get Real website or approach in two to four sentences, including what it does today and what is missing or not working well?

The current site is pretty limited and doesn’t do enough to guide students from curiosity to action. It has some basic information, but it doesn’t feel teen-friendly or engaging, and it doesn’t do a good job of connecting university courses, career possibilities, and real stories from people in computing. What’s missing most is a clearer path that helps students understand why computer science matters and what they can do next if they want to explore it further.
What current processes or website features do you want to change or improve most for this new Get Real site?

We most want to improve how students navigate the content and how quickly they can find information that feels relevant to them. Right now, the material can feel scattered or too academic, so we want a smoother experience that leads them through course options, career examples, and preparation advice in a more motivating way. We also want the stories and guidance to feel more relatable to teens, not just to people already sure about computer science.
Based on your description, should the new site also include a way for students to quickly identify which computer science topics, careers, or paths match their interests?

Yes, that would be very helpful. A quick way for students to see which topics or careers fit their interests could make the site feel much more personal and useful, especially for students who are curious but not yet committed. It doesn’t have to be a formal quiz, but some kind of guided path or matching feature would fit the goal well.
What are the main features or functions you want the new Get Real website to have?

We want it to give students clear information about computer science courses, possible careers, and what preparation they should focus on before college. It should also include stories or profiles from computing professionals so students can see real examples of different paths, and it should present everything in a way that feels engaging and easy to understand for teens. If possible, it should help students figure out where they fit and what to explore next without feeling overwhelming.

So the main features/functions are: teen-friendly content, clear computer science course information, career guidance, preparation advice, real stories/profiles from computing professionals, and some kind of guided path or matching feature to help students identify relevant interests. Is that correct?
Yes, that’s correct. Those are the core things we want the new site to do, and the guided path or matching piece is especially important as long as it stays simple and easy for students to use.
Are there any other features you would like to see in this project, perhaps something not yet mentioned, such as a way for students to save useful pages or take a next step after exploring?

Saving useful pages or content would be nice if it’s not too complicated, and I can see value in giving students a clear next step after they explore, like where to learn more or who to contact. We haven’t fully defined those extras yet, so I’d want to check what’s practical and what the university wants to maintain.
Would you like the site to include a simple way for students to save or bookmark content for later use?

Yes, I think a simple save or bookmark feature would be useful. A lot of students may not finish exploring in one sitting, so being able to come back to pages they found interesting would help. It should be very lightweight, though, since we don’t want to add unnecessary complexity.
Would you like the site to include a clear next-step feature, such as suggested links, contacts, or actions after a student finishes exploring?

Yes, that would be a good idea. After students read about courses or careers, it would help to point them toward a next step, like related content, a contact, or another action they can take. We’d want it to feel supportive and not too pushy.
Could you prioritize the confirmed features and functions for me, from most important to least important?

At the top would be the teen-friendly content and the clear information about computer science courses, because those are the foundation of the site. Next would be the career guidance, preparation advice, and the professional stories or profiles, since those are what help students connect the information to real possibilities. After that I’d put the guided path or matching feature, and then the save/bookmark option and the clear next-step suggestions as useful but secondary enhancements.
For the teen-friendly content and clear course information, what should that part of the site accomplish for students?

It should make computer science feel understandable and relevant, not intimidating. Students should be able to quickly see what the courses are about, why they matter, and how they connect to real careers, using language and examples that feel approachable for high-schoolers.
How should the course information be organized so students can quickly understand it and relate it to real careers?

I think it should be organized in a very simple, scannable way, with short descriptions of what each course covers, what kind of skills it builds, and what careers it connects to. If possible, I’d like to see examples or little “why this matters” notes so students can connect a course to something concrete, like games, apps, cybersecurity, or data work.
For the career guidance, what do you want that feature to accomplish for students?

It should help students understand what people in computing actually do day to day and what kinds of jobs exist. We want it to broaden their view a little, especially for students who think computer science only means one narrow kind of job or who are not sure they belong in that field.
What details should each career example or profile include so students can understand the job clearly?

Each profile should give a plain-language job description, what a typical day looks like, the skills or classes that help, and maybe the kind of work setting or team they might be part of. It would also be helpful to include a real person’s background or path into the field, so students can see that there isn’t just one route.
For the preparation advice, what should students learn about how to get ready for college or a computer science path?

They should learn the practical basics, like what classes to take, how to build confidence with math and problem-solving, and what kinds of extracurricular or project experiences can help. We’d also want advice that reassures them that they don’t need to have everything figured out already, just a good next step.
What should the guided path or matching feature do to help students find content that fits their interests?

It should ask a few simple questions and then point students to the most relevant courses, career stories, and preparation advice. The main idea is to reduce overwhelm and help them start from whatever they already care about, whether that’s games, design, apps, hardware, or just figuring out what computer science even is.
For the save/bookmark feature, what should students be able to save, and how should they access it later?

They should be able to save the things that feel useful to them, like course pages, career profiles, and preparation tips. Later, they should have an easy place to come back and see their saved items together, so they can pick up where they left off without having to search again.
For the clear next-step suggestions, what should the site recommend after a student finishes exploring a topic?

It should suggest something small and relevant, like another course page, a related career profile, or a practical next action they can take right away. The goal is to keep them moving forward without making it feel like a big commitment.
Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project, and whose needs need to be considered, and why?

High school students are the primary audience, so their feedback matters most because the site has to feel approachable and useful to them. We also need input from university advisers, faculty, and current students or recent grads, since they can help make the content accurate, realistic, and encouraging.
What would a successful launch of this website look like for the Oregon University System?

A successful launch would mean students can easily find their way through the site, understand what computer science can lead to, and feel more confident about taking the next step. From our side, success would also look like the content being clear, teen-friendly, and useful enough that schools and advisers are comfortable pointing students to it.
